description: We are putting together Team Lunaris for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to build an awesome lunar mission planning tool and we are looking for passionate people to join us whether you are an expert ready to lead or a fresher who is eager to learn code and design alongside us so if you want to team up and build something incredible together let us know
summary:
The Story
South pole missions operate on razor-thin margins. Shifting a site by hundreds of meters or missing a launch window by days can plunge a lander into permanent shadow or cut off communication.
Current tools like NASA Quickmap offer deep data, but they lack quick, agile scenario comparison. When delays force a pivot, engineers need a fast way to evaluate alternatives. That is why we built LUNARISE.
What It Does
LUNARISE is an interactive web dashboard bridging complex spaceflight data and rapid decision-making. Planners and students can use it as a live sandbox to evaluate sites instantly.
Users can:
 * Compare Sites Side by Side: Weigh trade-offs across Apollo sites, CLPS targets, or coordinates.
 * Visualize Horizon Paths: Track the Sun and Earth relative to local terrain.
 * Monitor Power and Comms: Check solar elevation angles and visibility windows.
 * Scrub Through Time: Watch lighting shift across lunar days.
The Tech
Powered by NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA datasets.
details: LUNARISE Lunar Landing Site Navigator **Summary** LUNARISE is a web based mission planning dashboard that helps anyone choose where and when to land on the Moon. It answers two questions that decide whether a lunar mission survives. Will the Sun reach the solar panels and can the lander see Earth to send and receive radio signals. The whole tool is one self contained HTML file that runs in any modern browser on a laptop or a phone with no installation and no internet connection. **The Problem** Near the lunar south pole the Sun never rises more than about one and a half degrees above the horizon. Mountains and crater rims throw shadows that can last for weeks. Earth also appears to wobble in the lunar sky by about seven degrees because of libration, so a site that sees Earth today may lose the link tomorrow. A few kilometres or a few days can change a mission from healthy to dead. Today this analysis is spread across expert tools that are hard for students teachers and early stage teams to use. **What LUNARISE Does** You pick a landing site and a date and time in universal time. LUNARISE then calculates the position of the Sun and Earth in that site's sky and tells you whether terrain is blocking either one. It shows how much time is left before sunset and before Earth sets, how sunlit the site is across a full lunar month, how long the longest blackout lasts, and an overall site score from zero to one hundred. **Main Features** Mission view shows a headline status such as power and link nominal, a glowing sphere with the Sun elevation, seven day chips showing how sunny each coming day is, and six live readouts for Sun height, solar power, time to sunset, Earth height, time to Earth set and site score. A horizon panorama shows what an astronaut would see standing at the site with the terrain silhouette, the Sun and Earth. A body hidden behind terrain is dimmed and dashed. A sky dome shows the same view looking straight up. A terrain panel shows slope, slope direction, horizon relief, illumination, temperature range, hazard density and science return. A lander slope limit slider flags sites that are too steep and the slope aware power option tilts the solar panel to match the ground. Nudge buttons move a site about seven kilometres or half a degree so users can see how a small change affects the score. A launch slip table shows sunlight, Earth visibility and blackout length if the landing is delayed by seven, fourteen or twenty nine and a half days. A comparison matrix places up to six sites side by side with the best value in every row marked with a star. A south polar map shows the sites from above the pole with the Sun and Earth directions and live status. A timeline shows thirty days ahead and a seasons chart shows twelve lunar months. Time controls let users step by hour or day, jump a full lunar day and play the animation. Users can also enter any custom latitude and longitude and get the same analysis. Planner mode shows every table and control while Explorer mode hides the technical parts and keeps a plain language story so the tool works for the public and for classrooms. **Sites Included** Thirteen sites are built in. They include Shackleton de Gerlache Ridge, Malapert Massif, Haworth Rim, Nobile Rim 1, Faustini Rim A, Mons Mouton Plateau, Malapert A, Shiv Shakti, Von Karman, Mare Crisium, Tranquility Base, Taurus Littrow and Reiner Gamma. They cover Artemis candidate regions, commercial lunar payload missions and earlier landing sites. **Site Score** The score blends five factors. Sunlit time counts for thirty percent, Earth visibility for twenty five percent, science value for twenty percent, gentle slope for fifteen percent and low hazard for ten percent. A site that exceeds the chosen slope limit loses its slope credit. **How It Works** The Sun and Earth positions are calculated live in the browser. The model uses the mean lunar month of 29.53 days, the small seasonal swing of the subsolar latitude, Earth libration in longitude and latitude and a parallax correction for the Moon to Earth distance. Spherical trigonometry turns these into elevation and azimuth at each site. Each site has a terrain horizon profile and a body only counts as visible when it is above that horizon. The dashboard samples every hour across a lunar month to produce sunlit percentage, Earth visibility, blackout length and power statistics. **Data and Honesty** Sun and Earth positions come from an analytic orbital model and are accurate enough for planning exploration but not for mission certification. Slope, hazard, science value, temperature and horizon relief values are planning estimates prepared for this prototype and the horizon shapes are synthetic. We used NASA JPL Horizons, LROC QuickMap, NASA Moon Trek and the Canadian Space Agency moon exploration pages as the reference tools for checking and for the next version. The plan is to replace the estimates with real lunar orbiter elevation and illumination data. **Design** The interface uses a dark glass style inspired by mission control. It has frosted panels, high contrast text, clear keyboard focus, labels for screen readers and a layout that adapts from desktop to phone. **Who It Is For** Mission planners and students can compare sites and test schedule risk. Teachers can show why the lunar poles are hard. The public can explore the Moon through Explorer mode. **Next Steps** Ingest real lunar elevation, slope and illumination maps from LROC and Moon Trek. Connect live JPL Horizons ephemeris. Add a three dimensional surface view. Add radio relay and communication satellite coverage. Add more sites and downloadable mission reports. **Team** Team LUNARISE NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
